rows.question: What kinds of old photos do users struggle to retrieve?
rows.restated: What kinds of old photos do users struggle to retrieve?
rows.text:
**About a third of the cases where people only vaguely remembered an old photo ended with them finding it, and the single common first failure was that they searched for a real detail but search did not return it — about a quarter of cases.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

Across 115 cases of half-remembered photos, 38 found the photo and 31 first failed because search did not bring up a detail that really was in the picture. Other first failures were the photo already gone (20 cases), not using the search box (9), the photo being hard to spot in results (9), or not remembering enough to search (6). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:_all]]

A likely reason is people often have a concrete but brief memory (a face, place, object) and expect search to match it; when that expectation fails, it blocks the find. My read is that improving short-query matching would help the largest group. This is a small, public-post sample and not a rate for all people. [[analysis_funnel|collected]][[analysis_funnel|kept]][[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]]

*Want to see what people actually typed when search failed?*

rows.question: What information do people actually remember about a photo?
rows.restated: What information do people actually remember about a photo?
rows.gap: two AI readers went through the stories separately and agreed too rarely on what they actually remember about the photo to rely on it
dropped: The posts also show smaller counts for other memory types: about a quarter named the main subject in a single line of their post, about one in six said when it was taken, roughly one in ten named who was in it, and similar single-digit shares named photo type, objects, place or activity.
Unfortunately, the two AI readers agreed too rarely on what each person actually remembered to treat finer splits as reliable, so treat the smaller counts as tentative.
rows.text:
**People who only vaguely remembered a photo most often recalled what was in the picture — about two in five of the 115 cases said so.** [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

My read is that people lean first on the image content — subjects, objects, visible text — rather than precise dates or relationships; that explains why searches for words on posters or objects sometimes succeed or fail in the logs. [[story|90c8b5f8d8913d764335d981d06c5dc02200c937:0]][[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]][[story|112f493208a69edd002fcc3b5194ae1643a18c55:0]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed or wrote about what they remembered?*

rows.question: What information have people forgotten about the photo they want?
rows.restated: What kinds of details (what, when, who, where, event, etc.) did people say they had forgotten about the photo they were trying to find?
rows.text:
**People most often forgot what was in the photo; about two in five of the cases say they did, while forgetting when or where was less frequent (about one in eight forgot the date, about one in twenty forgot the exact place).** [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:when:core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=date_or_year@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=exact_place_or_venue_name@photo_class:_all]]

The posts show that in these half‑remembered hunts people most often retain a visual memory—objects, people or scenes—rather than temporal or locational details, so they type or search for content like “bicycle” or “bookshelf” and rely on that to lead them to the date. [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]][[story|59e9a7f78d915872a1fbf7ac64a747d4805810a6:0]] My read is that this shapes how they search: they reach for what they still recall (the subject), and then use that hit to recover missing facts like the date. 

A likely reason is that memory for content is stronger than memory for metadata (when or which venue), so improving ways to pivot from a content match to nearby photos by time or place would help the largest group. This inference is modest — the posts over‑represent problems and cannot tell us why search missed in technical terms. [[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see the exact words people typed when they looked for a photo?*

rows.question: How do users formulate searches when their memory is incomplete?
rows.restated: How do users formulate searches when their memory is incomplete?
rows.text:
**About a quarter of people who only half-remember a photo first typed a single word into search, and only a handful used a full natural description or a name.** The posts that say what was typed show single words like "vomit", "bicycle", "passport", "dog" or "photo frames" as first tries, and only 1 case reports a full sentence and 1 case reports typing a name [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=full_natural_description@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=named_entity@photo_class:_all]][[story|88a83897e2c872e72ac85967d7fc5c158d43bbb0:0]][[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]][[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]][[story|c06874c9c9acadf8038072c41b2d0d2c08c2bc10:0]][[story|c0d1dafa88ec6dba2c4741ebdda4c7a72aed14ac:0]]. 

Reading the path the study used, this pattern matters because in roughly a third of these cases the photo was found and in roughly a quarter the first failure was that people searched for something that truly was in the image but search did not bring it up [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]. My read is that many people simplify their half-memory to a single salient word first (a likely reason: speed or uncertainty), which makes their first query short and brittle. So improving how short single-word queries are interpreted would probably help a large group of these cases. 

I'm afraid the posts can't tell us exactly why search missed those photos or whether longer phrasing would have succeeded in each case, so interviews or controlled tests are needed to confirm what change helps most [[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]].

*Want to see the exact words people typed first?*

rows.question: Does Google Photos fail to understand the clues people give it?
rows.restated: Does Google Photos fail to understand the clues people give it?
rows.text:
**Yes — for people who only vaguely remembered a photo, about a quarter first failed because they searched for a detail that really was in the picture but search did not bring it up.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

That figure comes straight from the 115 cases about half-remembered photos we read: in 31 of those cases the first thing to go wrong was exactly that — the person typed a correct detail and search didn’t surface the photo. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] Other ways the hunt broke include the photo being gone (about one in six cases) and hard-to-spot results or no use of the search box. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]]

My read is that improving how short, concrete queries are matched would help the largest single group in these cases: better handling of brief object, person or text queries is likely to let more people reach the photo without extra steps. This is a cautious suggestion — we cannot see why search missed from these posts, and public posts over-represent failures, so this shows where fixes would reach the biggest group in this sample, not overall users. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]]

*Want to see what people actually typed when search first failed them?*

rows.question: What is Google Photos' annual revenue?
rows.restated: What is Google Photos' annual revenue?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
I'm afraid the posts about people hunting for photos do not contain financial information, so they cannot say what Google Photos' annual revenue is. The study is about users' search journeys and where those searches go wrong, not about product-level earnings.

*Would you like me to pull together what the study does show about where searches most often go wrong?*

rows.question: How many people use Ask Photos every month?
rows.restated: How many people use Ask Photos every month?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
I'm afraid the posts can't settle that: the study reads public posts about hunting for single photos and contains no telemetry or user counts, so it cannot say how many people use Ask Photos each month. It only records whether an author mentions their own frequency in a post; it cannot be turned into a monthly active‑user figure.

*Want me to pull the posts that mention how often an individual wrote they used the search?*

rows.question: What is the success rate for searches from vague memories?
rows.restated: What proportion of searches that start from vague memories succeed in finding the target photo?
withheld: share stated as a rate of users or searches: success rate
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.draft:
I'm afraid the posts can’t give a success rate for searches from vague memories: they are a non‑representative collection of public anecdotes without denominators or user counts, so you can't turn them into a proportion of searches or users. The study can report how many of the collected cases ended with the person finding the photo, but that count cannot be interpreted as a success rate for all searches or users.

*Want the count of cases that ended with the photo being found?*
rows.text:
I'm sorry — that's outside what this study can answer. It reads public posts in which people describe hunting for a photo they half-remember, and these are public cases, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them.

*Would you like to know instead where those searches most often go wrong?*

rows.question: Do Android users struggle to find photos more than iPhone users?
rows.restated: Do Android users struggle to find photos more than iPhone users?
rows.gap: the posts do not reliably say which phone people use, so there is no Android vs iPhone split
dropped: That said, the evidence lets us say where the evidence comes from and how thin device info is: most raw posts came from YouTube comments and X, and only a minority of cases mention whose phone or who searched, so platform is not recorded for a firm split.
rows.text:
I'm afraid the posts do not reliably record whether people used Android or iPhone, so we cannot compare struggles by platform directly. [[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

My read is that any apparent Android/iPhone pattern in these public posts would be driven by where people post, not by the phone they used: the study over-represents certain sites and people who post when things go wrong, so platform comparisons would be misleading. [[analysis_sources|youtube]][[analysis_sources|x]][[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]]

If you want a fair Android vs iPhone comparison, we need data that records device reliably (or interviews that ask it); the current posts simply can't settle that. [[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

*Want me to pull the cases that do say whose phone was used so you can see their text?*

rows.question: Has search got worse since Ask Photos launched?
rows.restated: Has search got worse since Ask Photos launched?
problems: closing: the answer does not end with one italic closing question
rows.gap: the stories were not compared across time, so there is no before-and-after
rows.text:
**The posts cannot tell us whether search has got worse since Ask Photos launched; they do show that in about a quarter of narrowly read cases search failed to surface a correct detail people typed.** [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

Why I say that — the data come from public posts, not a before‑and‑after comparison, so the study cannot settle a change over time. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]] What the study does show is how often the first thing to go wrong, in 115 cases where people only vaguely remembered a photo, was that they searched for something that truly was in the photo yet search did not bring it up — about a quarter of those cases. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

My read is that this points to a sizable set of half‑remembered hunts where search did not return the matching photo; fixing whatever part of search misses correct, typed details would help that group. (A likely reason is that these posts over‑represent failures, so the real-world share could be smaller.) [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Would you like to see the actual phrases people typed first, or the other places the path broke? *Want to see what people typed first?*

rows.question: Is Apple Photos search better than Google Photos search at finding old photos?
rows.restated: Is Apple Photos search better than Google Photos search at finding old photos?
rows.gap: the stories do not compare how well other photo apps search
rows.text:
**No — the study cannot say whether Apple Photos is better; its posts only report people’s experiences with Google Photos, so there’s no comparable data to judge one app against the other.** [[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

That said, the study does show where Google Photos trips people who vaguely remember a photo: in the 115 cases about a half-remembered photo, roughly two in five found it straight away and about one in ten found it after a struggle, while about half of the cases don’t say how they ended — so the public posts most often record trouble but not a complete outcome. [[analysis_crosstab|core.outcome=found@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.outcome=found_after_struggle@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.outcome=not_stated@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

My read is that the visible problems are about how people put memories into words and what search then showed them: posts complain search returns many irrelevant matches (“listing too many photos with no dog”, “way too many images of my shop”) or the wrong face or category (“it found photos of my cats instead of me with beard journey”, “this is the picture google photos thought I was looking for”). [[story|c06874c9c9acadf8038072c41b2d0d2c08c2bc10:0]][[story|0ef3821f2d59998617a4b53f428fd49c9a22d2ff:0]][[story|3ba2ad97300ec1206044dc3deed79e0240a13297:1]][[story|a8eaefe2e0199103bba08d2d1f34aad86d3267a5:0]]

Because the evidence doesn’t include Apple Photos cases, interviews or instrumented comparisons would be needed to know which app is better and why.

*Want to see what people actually typed when they tried to find a photo?*

rows.question: How deep do people scroll through search results before deciding?
rows.restated: How deep do people scroll through search results before deciding?
rows.gap: few public posts say anything about how far down the results they went — 2 of 115 stories do — so it is left for interviews with real users
dropped: So I’m afraid the posts can’t settle how deep people usually scroll; that question is left for interviews with real users.
rows.text:
**Very little in the public posts says how far people scrolled — only two cases report it, one saying a few scrolls and one saying all the way down.** [[analysis_coverage|6.6]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:6.6=a_few_scrolls@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:6.6=exhaustive@photo_class:_all]]

My read is that the evidence most often records where the hunt first failed (for example, about a third found the photo, about a quarter say search didn’t bring up a correct detail, and about one in six found the photo was gone), not how far people inspected results afterward, so scrolling depth is rarely mentioned. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]]

Because the posts are skewed toward problems and give almost no consistent detail on result depth, the only responsible next step is targeted user interviews or instrumented logs to measure how many results people view and when they stop. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

*Want me to pull together the two posts that do describe scrolling so you can see their exact words?*

rows.question: How often does a wrong year act as a hard filter that hides the photo?
rows.restated: How often does a wrong year act as a hard filter that hides the photo?
rows.gap: few public posts say anything about whether the system discarded the photo because one detail was wrong — 22 of 290 stories do — so it is left for interviews with real users
rows.text:
**The posts cannot settle whether a wrong year acts as a hard filter, because only a small slice of cases even mention a system discarding a photo for one wrong detail.** The study found only 22 of 290 cases say anything about whether the system discarded the photo because one detail was wrong, so the public posts alone are too thin to answer this reliably [[analysis_coverage|5.3]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]. 

What we can say about the vaguely remembered-photo group: in that group, two cases say a small mistake in a detail did not matter and one says adding more words made the photo disappear — these are single, isolated examples in the 115 cases about vague memories, so treat them as hints not conclusions [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.3=soft_ok@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.3=and_logic_shrinks_recall@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]. My read is that public posts point to both outcomes (a wrong detail sometimes not blocking a match, sometimes coinciding with disappearance), but they are far too few to show how often a wrong year acts as a hard filter. 

If you want frequency or causal detail, interviews or instrumented logs are needed; the posts simply do not supply that evidence [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]].

*Want to see the 22 posts that mention a detail being wrong so we can inspect what people actually wrote?*

rows.question: How many attempts do people make before they give up?
rows.restated: How many attempts do people make before they give up?
rows.gap: two AI readers went through the stories separately and agreed too rarely on how long they kept trying to rely on it
dropped: My read is that most people who wrote about it either gave a single attempt or did not state how long they tried; however, the two AI readers disagreed too often on duration coding for us to rely on more detailed splits.
rows.text:
**30 of the 115 cases say how long the person kept trying; of those, 21 say they tried once, 6 say they tried a few times over minutes, and three say they tried an hour or more.** [[analysis_coverage|8.1]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=one_attempt@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=few_attempts_minutes@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=hour_or_more@photo_class:_all]]

That is the best the posts can tell us: only 30 cases report any duration at all, so the pattern — about two‑thirds one try, about one in five a few minutes, and a handful an hour or more — comes from that subset. [[analysis_coverage|8.1]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=one_attempt@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=few_attempts_minutes@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=hour_or_more@photo_class:_all]]

If you want, I can pull the exact phrases people typed when they described trying once versus longer — the posts include short lines like “it pulled it up instantly” and “No matter how many times I look back…” that show how they reported effort. [[story|a2d48f97439d430f6d2399321a058252025a6085:0]][[story|3f6c7b626f52b658b0c519881ff8cb6967208570:0]]

*Want to see the 30 posts that say how long they kept trying?*

rows.question: Why does Ask Photos fail most often?
rows.restated: Why does Ask Photos fail most often?
rows.text:
**Ask Photos most often fails because people search for a real detail in the photo and search does not bring it up — this was the first thing to go wrong in about a quarter of the cases.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

The evidence shows that, among the 115 cases where someone only vaguely remembered a photo, the single commonest first failure was search not returning a photo that actually contained the thing they typed. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] My read is that this matters because these people could put a correct, specific detail into words — the memory problem was not “couldn’t remember enough” — yet the system did not surface that photo for them. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

This suggests prioritising improvements that help the search box find photos when people type short, correct details: for example stronger matching on objects, text on images, or short phrases. A likely reason is that better reading of short queries would reach the largest group of failing cases. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

I’m afraid the posts can’t settle why search missed each time (we only see what people wrote, not internal search behaviour). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see exactly what people typed when search first failed?*

rows.question: Since most failures happen because the photo was deleted, what should Google fix first?
rows.restated: Since most failures happen because the photo was deleted, what should Google fix first?
withheld: unsupported number (a share in words does not fit): the majority
rows.draft:
Bold correction — the posts cannot show that most failures happen because the photo was deleted — the photo‑gone problem appears in about one in six cases, not the majority [[analysis_opportunity|stage0]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]]. 

Fix first — improve search’s handling of simple, partial cues — the single biggest first failure is that people searched for something actually in the photo but search did not bring it up, which is about a quarter of the cases [[analysis_opportunity|stage5]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]. My read is that fixing this yields the largest immediate win: better matching of short nouns, concepts and named entities would turn many first‑tries that now fail into finds. This follows because the study traced each hunt step and ranked where it first failed; that step is the only one large enough to rank [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_opportunity|stage5]][[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:top]]. 

What it means — prioritize query interpretation, tolerant boolean logic, and richer concept/entity indexing and then test those fixes in interviews that focus on sentimental and unclear photos where these failures cluster [[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:intelligence_needed]][[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:target_segment]]. I’m afraid the posts can’t tell us why the engine missed any single query internally or how users in other demographics would behave [[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]].

*Want to see what people actually typed first?*

rows.question: What share of utility-photo stories end with the person giving up?
rows.restated: What proportion of stories about practical photos end with the person giving up?
rows.gap: only 21 stories are about photos kept for the information in them (receipts, documents, notes) — too few (under 30) for a percentage, so only counts are given
rows.text:
**Very few — only four of the 21 utility-photo cases end with the person giving up.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]]

Those 21 cases are the small group kept for the information in them (receipts, documents, notes), so I can only give counts, not a share. The posts show that in eight of those 21 the photo was already gone, in six they found it, in four they could not remember enough to search, and in three search failed to bring it up. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

My read is that for these information photos the main problems are the image being absent or people not remembering enough to form a query; giving up appears relatively uncommon in this small set. A likely reason is that missing backups or weak memory stop the search before prolonged attempts do. This is tentative — the group is small, so treat it as a hint. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]]

*Want to see the posts where people say the photo was gone or where they found it?*

rows.question: What share of stories about photos kept for both sentimental and practical reasons fail at search?
rows.restated: What proportion of stories about photos that were kept for both sentimental and practical reasons involve a failure at search (i.e., the finding the photo journey went wrong before reaching the 'nothing went wrong' end)?
rows.gap: no stories bear on this in detail; none of the stories is about photos kept both as memories and for the information in them, so nothing can be said about them
rows.text:
**I’m afraid the posts can’t settle that: none of the cases is about photos kept both for sentimental and for practical reasons, so the study has no direct count for that group.** [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]]

What the evidence does allow is this: we can describe the nearby groups the study did cover and how they failed at search. For photos kept as memories (people, trips, events), about a third of cases found the photo and about a quarter first failed because the person searched for something that really was in the photo but search did not bring it up — a small group, so treat these as rough guides. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:sentimental]] For photos kept for information (receipts, documents, notes), the most frequent single first problem was that the photo was already gone — counts only. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

My read is that if you need a figure for mixed-purpose photos, we’d need cases that explicitly say the photo was kept both for memory and for information; without those, any share would be a guess.

*Want me to pull the posts about photos kept as memories so you can see the exact failure phrases people used?*

rows.question: How many core stories are there, and from how many different people?
rows.restated: How many stories about a vaguely remembered photo are in the stories, and from how many distinct people did those stories about a vaguely remembered photo come?
rows.text:
**There are 115 core cases told by 109 different people.** [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

That is the set the study treats as the half‑remembered or "vaguely remembered" photo cases; the 115 count is the number of cases, and those cases were written by 109 people. [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

A likely reason the two counts differ is that a few people posted more than one such case, but the posts themselves give the case and author counts directly. [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]][[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]]

*Want to see how many of those cases said where the photo first went wrong?*

rows.question: How many core stories first go wrong because search did not understand or match what was typed?
rows.restated: How many stories about a vaguely remembered photo had their first problem at the step where search failed to understand or match what the user typed?
rows.text:
**31 of the 115 core cases first went wrong because the person searched for something that really was in the photo but search did not bring it up.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

That is about a quarter of the cases about a photo the person only vaguely remembered, so this single failure point is a sizable fraction of the problems our posts describe. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] My read is that improving how short, concrete queries are matched to photo content would directly help this group: they had a correct detail in mind, typed it, and still didn't see the photo. (I should say the posts cannot tell us why search missed it internally.) [[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see what people actually typed when this happened?*

rows.question: And how does that split by kind of photo?
rows.restated: How does the place where finding the photo first goes wrong differ by kind of photo (sentimental, practical, both, unclear)?
rows.text:
**The split by kind of photo can't show a clear difference — the groups are too small to compare, so I can only describe each kind on its own.** [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

For photos kept as memories (people, trips, events): in this subset, about a third of cases say nothing went wrong — they found the photo — and about a quarter name that search failed to surface a correct detail first; smaller counts name the photo being gone or that they never used the search box. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=1@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:sentimental]]

For photos where the post does not say why they were kept: about a third report search failed to surface a correct detail first, and about a third found the photo; smaller counts say the photo was gone or hard to spot among results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:unclear]]

For photos kept for their information (receipts, documents, notes): counts only — the largest single first failure is the photo already being gone (8 cases); 6 cases found the photo; four cases say the person couldn't remember enough; three cases report search failed to surface a correct detail. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

My read is that improving how search handles correct short queries would help across these kinds because the same failure (search not surfacing a correct detail) appears in each group.

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed when search failed?*

rows.question: Does that differ for utility photos?
rows.restated: Do people type different first queries when searching for practical photos compared with other kinds of photos?
rows.gap: the stories hold nothing on how this differs by kind of photo
dropped: That said, the evidence does tell us what limited things it can: 76 of the 290 cases say anything about what people typed first, but none of the facts link those first-typed queries to photo kinds like utility photos, so we cannot compare groups.
rows.text:
**I’m afraid the posts don’t let us say whether people who look for utility photos behave differently — the cases hold nothing on how this differs by kind of photo.** [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

My read is that we can still use the raw examples as hints about what people try when they do look for utility items: posts show single-word labels like "passport", "driver's license", "photo frames", "Boba" and short object names were typed first. [[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]][[story|765749899f7fa8a7f4c8527cc2337029e134b9ce:0]][[story|c0d1dafa88ec6dba2c4741ebdda4c7a72aed14ac:0]][[story|cbc995976ab0e7519ef70d4d3bf1b20c0485baf8:0]] This suggests (reasoning) people often start with a concise object word when they remember a clear object. But treat that as a tentative cue, not evidence the behaviour differs for utility photos specifically.

rows.question: give me the entire retrieval journey of a vaguely remembered photo. Then tell me where is the biggest problem
rows.restated: give me the entire finding the photo journey of a vaguely remembered photo. Then tell me where is the biggest problem
problems: closing: the answer does not end with one italic closing question
rows.draft:
**Answer: the retrieval journey runs as a clear path of steps, and in roughly a quarter of the cases the first thing that went wrong was that people searched for a correct detail but search did not bring the photo up.** 

Start to finish the team read each case along the path: was the photo present at all → why they wanted it → what they remembered and forgot → where they looked (search box or scrolling) → how they put the memory into words → whether search returned matches → whether they spotted it among results → retrying or giving up → how it ended. Each case was coded for the first step that failed. 

What the evidence shows about where things first went wrong: in about a third of cases the person found the photo (38 cases). In about a quarter the first failure was search not returning a photo that actually contained the searched detail (31 cases). In about one in six the photo was already gone (20 cases). In about one in ten people never used the search box (9 cases). In about one in ten the photo was in results but hard to spot (9 cases). In about one in twenty the person could not remember enough to search (6 cases). Two cases only reported why they were looking, not a failure point. 

My read is that the single biggest problem to fix is the quarter where search failed to surface a photo that matched the detail they typed: improving how short, specific queries map to photos would reach the largest group of failing cases and so likely reduce the most complaints. A likely reason is that these posts show people put a correct, testable clue into words but did not see the matching photo returned, so better matching of such queries should help. This is based on what people wrote; I’m afraid the posts cannot show why search missed internally. 

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed or the cases where search failed first?*

rows.question: Show which words people tried first.
rows.restated: Which words or queries did people try first when searching for a remembered photo?
rows.text:
**People often typed a single word first — about a quarter of the cases that say what they typed begin with one word.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]]

Three short examples the posts give: “searched ‘forest’ in my gallery” (looking for old fall photos; first result) [[story|346adeec584d4ac2df9090145e995deb4acb616e:0]]; “search Google Photos for ‘bicycle’” (could find the photo) [[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]]; “I just search for ‘passport’” (found passport copies without labelling) [[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]]. [[story|346adeec584d4ac2df9090145e995deb4acb616e:0]][[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]][[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]]

Together these show that when people half‑remember a photo they commonly try a short, single-word clue first — often an object or noun — rather than a phrase or full description. My read is that short single-word queries are the natural, easy thing people try first; that suggests improving how single-word queries match specific visual details would help the largest identified group. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]]

**People looking for receipts say things like "receipt returned nothing", "returned way too many images", and "automatically deleted" — in our posts these exact phrases show what went wrong.** [[story|probe-inj-04]][[story|0ef3821f2d59998617a4b53f428fd49c9a22d2ff:0]][[story|a9267da0c42d4f499c22c934d3f214f68f75c0d4:0]]

- "it returned way too many images of my shop." — the person searched "scrap" for a scrap receipt and got many irrelevant photos instead. [[story|0ef3821f2d59998617a4b53f428fd49c9a22d2ff:0]]  
- "They're is nothing in my trash bin." / "The rest were automatically deleted." — the person reports older images missing from their library, not found anywhere. [[story|a9267da0c42d4f499c22c934d3f214f68f75c0d4:0]]

Together these posts show three distinct problems people report when a receipt search fails: the query yields no results, it yields many irrelevant matches, or the photo is gone. rows.question: What happens when people search for a pet photo and cannot find it?
rows.restated: What happens when people search for a pet photo and cannot find it?
rows.text:
**About a quarter of these cases first failed because people searched for something that really was in the photo, but search did not bring it up.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

Quoted phrases and context —
- "dog park" — the person searched but the photo of their dog at the park did not appear (post about failing to find a dog photo). [[story|probe-inj-06]]  
- "bicycle" — the person says they searched that word to find a photo (example of typing an object name). [[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]]  
- "threw them up immediately" — the person searched words on posters and Google Photos returned the photo fast (an instance where text-in-photo worked). [[story|90c8b5f8d8913d764335d981d06c5dc02200c937:0]]

Together these show that people look for pets by typing objects or short phrases (like location or visible words), and sometimes that finds the photo and sometimes it does not: about a quarter of the vaguely remembered pet-photo cases report the search term should have matched but did not. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] My read is that improving how short, concrete queries (objects, locations, text seen in the image) are matched and surfaced would help the largest single group of failing cases.
